title: Ask again (2:9)
hookLine: if refused, return with three friends, up to three times
tomorrow: and when you're the one asked, how fast should you say yes?

cards: "Not yet." Two words on a lock screen, after the sorry you worked up the nerve to send. What if you ask, and they say no?
One instinct says give up, you tried. Another says keep asking, tonight, until they cave. Maimonides has a third answer, and it's oddly precise.
One question for today: how many times do you have to ask?

teach.b: In the same halakhah as yesterday, he writes: if the one you wronged doesn't want to forgive, bring three of their friends, and go to them together, and ask. If they refuse, come back a second time, and a third.
If they still refuse, you may leave them be. And then the line that turns the whole thing around: the one who won't forgive is now the one in the wrong.
There's one exception. If the person is your teacher, Maimonides says, go even a thousand times. Notice what the friends are for.
Not a mob. People the other person trusts, who can say: this is real, you can open the door. And notice the limit.
Asking is a duty, but it isn't a siege. Now a neighbor.
Christians read a strikingly similar step in the Gospel of Matthew.
"If thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone." And if he won't hear, "take with thee one or two more."

Both traditions bring in a few trusted people when two alone get stuck, so a broken thing doesn't stay broken out of pride. The honest difference: in Matthew, the one who goes is the one who was wronged.
In Maimonides, it's the one who did the wrong, going to ask. Same few friends, walking in from opposite sides of the fight.

how: Jewish law treats asking forgiveness as an obligation with limits: the one who did wrong asks, returns with others if refused, and after three sincere tries is no longer bound to keep asking (Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:9).

o: keep asking forgiveness, with friends, up to three times
repeat a question until the teacher explains it
pray the same request until God answers it

p: go back with three of their friends
take with thee one or two more

s: if someone says no to your apology, you've done your part
Maimonides: go back with three of their friends, a second and a third time.
after three sincere tries, the one refusing is the one in the wrong
Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:9: the one who won't forgive is now the sinner.
in Matthew, the one who did wrong goes to ask forgiveness
in Matthew, the one who was wronged goes, first alone, then with one or two more.

games.q: you missed your best friend's recital and apologized. she said 'whatever' and has gone quiet for a week. you've asked once. what does Maimonides suggest now?
o: go back with a couple of friends she trusts, and ask again, sincerely.
message her every hour until she gives in and answers you.
stop; one sincere apology means the rest is now on her.
games.why: Maimonides: three friends, up to three times. asking is a duty, not a siege, and after that the refusal is hers to carry.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one door that closed on you after you asked. Without forcing anything, ask yourself who the other person trusts, and what a calmer second ask might sound like. Hold that picture until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Ask again: Maimonides' rule when forgiveness is refused. Return with three friends, up to three times; then the refusal is theirs to carry.

orig.note: Hebrew: forgiveness, the pardon one person grants another.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: ask again, but not tonight, not alone, and not forever. Day fifteen forty-six, still asking.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:9 (three friends, three times; the refuser becomes the sinner; a teacher, even a thousand times)
Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 87a (asking forgiveness before three rows of people, up to three times)
